content.title: About
content.content: Parmesan is a hard, aged cheese from Italy made from cow’s milk. It is traditionally aged 12–36 months, developing a granular texture and a nutty, fruity, and buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parmesan holds a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status – it can only be produced in specific Italian regions.
Grated Parmesan is a staple topping in cuisines worldwide.
Traditional Parmesan is made from whole cow’s milk without added cream.
Extra‑aged Parmesan (over 24 months) develops a more crystalline structure and a sharper taste.
In Italy, Parmesan is sometimes served as “parmesan balls” – small dough balls coated with grated cheese.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Parmesan provides about 1,100 mg of calcium per 100 g, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: It contains roughly 35 g of protein per 100 g, aiding muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Fermentation introduces beneficial bacteria that can support gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: Long aging breaks down most lactose, making Parmesan often tolerable for those with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to Parmesan.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Parmesan contains about 650 mg of sodium per 30 g serving, so those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: At roughly 430 kcal per 100 g, it should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Parmesan is typically grated over pasta, risotto, soups, and salads. It can also be served in small shards as a snack, paired with fruit, nuts, or honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Parmesan in its original packaging or wrapped in parchment paper and then a loose‑fit plastic bag in the refrigerator at 4–7 °C. For longer storage, it can be frozen wrapped in foil, though texture may change.
